sections.h2: Which Lee County offices deal with a property tax bill?
sections.html:
Four offices in Dixon share the work, and the right call depends on the question. Value and exemption questions go to the assessment office, bill and payment questions go to the Treasurer, and rate questions go to the County Clerk.

Lee County property tax offices as listed on the county website
OfficeHandlesContact
Treasurer and CollectorBills, payments, annual tax sale, senior tax deferral815-288-4477, 112 E Second Street, mail to P.O. Box 328
Chief County Assessment OfficeAssessments, exemptions, appeal forms815-288-4483, 112 E Second Street, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays
Board of ReviewHears assessment complaints815-288-4483, meets in the assessment office
County Clerk and RecorderTax rate extension, redemption after a tax sale, deeds815-288-3309, mail to P.O. Box 329

All four sit in the Old Lee County Courthouse on East Second Street. The Treasurer's page says the office collects and distributes more than $96 million a year among more than 130 taxing districts, so a single bill in Lee County is really a stack of schools, townships, fire districts and the county itself.

sections.h2: What kind of county is Lee County for a home seller?
sections.html:
Lee County is a mostly rural county in northern Illinois, organized in 1839 when the lower half of Ogle County was split off. Dixon is the county seat and largest city. Amboy is the other city the county lists, and Rochelle sits mostly in Ogle County. The land covers about 725 square miles and borders Ogle, DeKalb, LaSalle, Bureau and Whiteside counties.

The Census Bureau counts 32,914 residents as of July 1, 2025, down from 34,145 in the 2020 count. Owners occupy 73.6% of homes, the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $154,600, and median household income is $70,292. Only 32 building permits were issued in 2025, so most houses a buyer sees are older stock. Dixon's winters bring a January average low near 10 degrees, and an EF4 tornado touched down in the county on April 9, 2015, so storm history is a fair question for a buyer to ask.

School districts that touch the county include Dixon Unit 170, Amboy 272, Ashton 275, Lee Center 271, Polo 222 and Sterling 5. Your district sets a large part of the rate on your bill.

sections.h2: How does Lee County assess a house?
sections.html:
Township assessors set the values, and the Chief County Assessment Office compiles them. Residential property is assessed at 33 1/3% of fair cash value, and a notice is mailed when an individual parcel's assessment changes. A change caused only by an equalization factor, sometimes called a township multiplier, does not require a notice.

Illinois reassesses on a four-year cycle. The county's publication page says 2026 is the general (quadrennial) year for Amboy, Ashton, Bradford, Franklin Grove, Nachusa, Lee Center, May and Sublette townships. Property records, including square footage, age and lot size, can be reviewed at the assessment office, and the county posts a parcel search and property record cards online.

If your bill rose, the county's FAQ lists three general reasons: local governments voted a larger levy, you may be missing an exemption you qualify for, or neighbors gained exemptions you lack. Lee County has no power to set another district's levy. Under the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, most districts can raise their levy by the lesser of 5% or inflation over the highest extension of the prior three years, with exceptions for new construction, bonds and voter-approved referenda.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Lee County assessment?
sections.html:
You file a written complaint with the Lee County Board of Review within 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55). The county posted November 18, 2026 as the 2026 publication date for the townships listed above, with a filing deadline of December 18, 2026. Other townships follow their own publication dates, so confirm yours with the assessment office.

The Board has three members appointed by the County Board and can confirm, reduce or increase an assessment as appears just. Its rules recognize four kinds of argument:

  • Assessment equity compared with similar homes
  • Fair cash value
  • An incorrect physical description of the property
  • Matters of law

Talk with your township assessor or the assessment office first, because many questions end there. The only complaint that can be heard after the 30 days is a discrepancy in the physical data, such as a house described as larger than it is. A Board decision can be appealed to the state Property Tax Appeal Board, reachable at 217-782-6076 or at 401 S Spring Street, Room 402, Springfield. The Board rules on value, so a complaint about the size of the final bill belongs with the taxing districts instead.

sections.h2: How and when do you pay a Lee County tax bill?
sections.html:
Illinois bills real estate tax in two installments, and Lee County prints the due dates on each bill. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-15, the first installment becomes delinquent after the later of June 1 or the day after the printed date, and the second after the later of September 1 or the day after its printed date. Interest runs at 1 1/2% per month or part of a month. A payment postmarked on or before the due date is on time.

You can pay by several routes:

  • Online through the county's property tax inquiry site, where a pay link appears once you find your parcel by PIN, owner name or address.
  • By phone at 877-690-3729, using jurisdiction code 7042.
  • By mail to Lee County Collector, P.O. Box 328, Dixon, IL 61021.
  • In person at the Treasurer's office on East Second Street.

The third-party card fee is printed as 2.40% with a $2.00 minimum. E-check fees start at $2 for amounts up to $50,000 and rise in steps, as the county's due-dates page lists. A lost bill is not an excuse, so ask the Treasurer for a duplicate. Address changes go to the Treasurer on the county's change-of-address form.

sections.h2: Which Lee County exemptions and deferrals can lower the bill?
sections.html:
Exemptions reduce the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied. Lee County is not next to a county of 3,000,000 or more people, so the statute's lower dollar amounts apply here. The main ones are:

  • General homestead: up to $6,000 off equalized assessed value for an owner-occupied home (35 ILCS 200/15-175).
  • Senior citizens: up to $5,000 for an owner who is 65 by December 31 of the assessment year (35 ILCS 200/15-170). The county's form says the exemption renews automatically once approved, and the owner must report if the home stops qualifying.
  • Senior assessment freeze: needs an annual application and a household income under the limit printed on the county form.
  • Senior tax deferral: run by the Treasurer for owners 65 and older with household income up to $75,000, rising to $77,000 for tax year 2026 and $79,000 for 2027. Deferred tax becomes a lien that is paid when the home is sold.

Exemption applications go to the assessment office. When a home sells, state law keeps the homestead exemption in place for the rest of that assessment year, and the office may ask the new owner to apply for the next one.

sections.h2: What happens if Lee County property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
The county sells the unpaid tax, not the house. The Treasurer holds a tax sale at the end of each tax year for every parcel still unpaid. The owner keeps the right to redeem by paying the tax plus costs and interest, and redemption is handled by the Tax Redemption Department of the County Clerk's office.

The statute generally allows 3 years from the sale date to redeem, with exceptions listed in 35 ILCS 200/21-350. If a tax buyer holds your parcel, ask the Clerk for the exact redemption figure and last day before you agree to any sale price.

sections.h2: How is the tax handled when you sell a Lee County house?
sections.html:
The title company or closing attorney reads the current bill and any unpaid installments, then splits the year between seller and buyer on the settlement statement. Ask the Treasurer whether any earlier year is delinquent or sold, because that balance must be cleared or paid from the proceeds. If a mortgage servicer pays from escrow, confirm which installments it has already sent.

Sellers with inherited houses, tenants or deferred maintenance often have back taxes mixed in with those problems. A written payoff from the Treasurer, plus the Clerk's redemption figure when a sale has occurred, lets you compare offers on the same footing.

faqs.q: Who do I call in Lee County about my tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Lee County Treasurer at 815-288-4477 for bills and payments. The assessment office at 815-288-4483 answers value, exemption and appeal questions, and the County Clerk at 815-288-3309 covers how rates are developed and redemption after a tax sale.

faqs.q: Can I still appeal my Lee County assessment after the 30 days?
faqs.a: Generally no. Complaints to the Board of Review must be filed within 30 days after the roll is published. The county's FAQ names one exception, a mismatch in the physical description of the property, such as the wrong square footage.

faqs.q: How much is the general homestead exemption in Lee County?
faqs.a: Up to $6,000 off equalized assessed value, because Lee County is not contiguous to a county of 3,000,000 or more inhabitants. The statute is 35 ILCS 200/15-175, and applications go to the Chief County Assessment Office.

faqs.q: What interest applies to a late Lee County tax payment?
faqs.a: Interest is 1 1/2% per month or portion of a month under 35 ILCS 200/21-15, counted from the later of the statutory date or the day after the due date printed on the bill. A payment postmarked by the due date is on time.

faqs.q: Does the senior tax deferral cancel the tax?
faqs.a: No. The deferral postpones payment, and the deferred tax becomes a lien that is paid when the home is eventually sold. Owners must be 65 or older and apply through the Lee County Treasurer, who sets the household income limit printed on the county page.
